definition: Fitting a system to a specific test set by repeatedly making choices based on its results.
A single number that summarizes performance across all test cases, like overall accuracy.
A measure of how well a classifier separates positive from negative cases across all thresholds. 0.5 is chance, 1.0 is perfect.
The comparison point for a result: a simpler method, an older model, or the current human workflow.
Checking specific behaviors with targeted test cases, like whether a model's answer stays the same when a name is changed (Ribeiro et al., 2020).
A fixed dataset and scoring method used to compare systems on a task.

How well a system's confidence matches how often it's actually right. A calibrated model that says "90% sure" is right about 90% of the time. Modern neural networks are often overconfident (Guo et al., 2017).
Testing what a system can do, as opposed to how people use it or what effects it has.
When a human-AI team does better than either the human or the AI alone (Bansal et al., 2021).
A range that likely contains the true value of a measurement, given sampling noise.
An abstract quality you want to measure but can't observe directly, like reasoning or helpfulness (Cronbach & Meehl, 1955).
How well a measurement actually captures the construct it claims to measure (Messick, 1995).
When test data, or close copies of it, appear in a model's training data.
The way evaluation criteria change as people grade real outputs.
A standard document describing how a dataset was created, what's in it, and what it's suited for (Gebru et al., 2021).
Reporting results separately for different groups or input types instead of only as an average.
A difference between the data a system was built and tested on and the data it meets in use.
A benchmark that keeps adding new examples, often written to defeat current models.
The effort put into drawing out a model's full capability, through prompting, tools, fine-tuning, or scaffolding.
Grouping and studying a system's mistakes to understand their causes. Works best with precisely defined error groups, enough examples, and tested hypotheses (Wu et al., 2019).
An agreed-on acceptable failure rate, with an agreed-on response when it's exceeded. Borrowed from site reliability engineering (Beyer et al., 2016).
A model's ability to tell that it's being evaluated rather than used for real (Needham et al., 2025).
Testing a system on data from a different setting than the one it was developed in, ideally by an independent team.
The answer treated as correct in an evaluation. Often a human judgment with its own error.
Data kept separate from training and tuning so it can give an unbiased estimate of performance (Dwork et al., 2015).
How often independent human raters give the same judgment. Low agreement means the task, the instructions, or the construct needs work.
A public ranking of systems on one or more benchmarks.
Using a language model to grade or compare outputs from AI systems (Zheng et al., 2023).
A standard document describing a model's intended use, evaluation results, and limitations (Mitchell et al., 2019).
Randomly exposing some users to a change and comparing outcomes against users who didn't get it, often called an A/B test (Kohavi et al., 2020).
Accepting AI output when it's wrong. Its opposite, underreliance, is ignoring AI output when it's right (Parasuraman & Riley, 1997).
Asking raters which of two outputs is better, instead of scoring each on its own. Used at scale by preference arenas (Chiang et al., 2024).
The set of options where you can't improve one metric, like accuracy, without making another, like cost, worse.
pass@k is the chance of at least one success in k attempts. pass^k is the chance of success on all k attempts, a measure of consistency (Yao et al., 2025).
How much a model's results change with small changes to how a prompt is worded or formatted.
Deliberately trying to make a system fail or cause harm, to find problems before others do.
How consistent a measurement is when repeated. A measurement can be reliable and still not valid.
When an optimized system finds a way to score well on its objective without doing what the objective was meant to encourage.
A category that sets how much evaluation a system needs, based on its potential impact. Risk-based prioritization is central to the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (2023).
Strategic underperformance on an evaluation (van der Weij et al., 2025).
When top systems score near the maximum on a benchmark, so it no longer separates them.
Learning a pattern that predicts the right answer on the test without the intended skill (Geirhos et al., 2020).
Evaluating a system together with the people, workflows, and institutions around it.
Releasing a system to progressively larger groups of users while monitoring results at each step.
The chance an experiment detects a real difference of a given size. Small test sets have low power.
How well the evidence supports the interpretations and uses of a score (Messick, 1995).
Informal, exploratory trying-out of an AI system. Practitioners describe it as the first line of evaluation (van der Maden et al., 2026). Useful as a start, risky as the whole process.
